name: Chele La
image_query: Chele La pass prayer flags Bhutan
tagline: Bhutan's highest motorable pass, between Paro and Haa
meta_description: Chele La, Bhutan: the 3,988 m road pass between Paro and Haa, Jomolhari views, the Kila Goemba hike, ridge walks, snow closures, timing and costs.
summary: Chele La is the road pass between Paro and Haa, at about 3,988 m, usually described as the highest motorable pass in Bhutan. It is about 1.5 hours from Paro town. Come early on a clear morning for prayer flags and views of Jomolhari, walk the ridge or hike down to Kila Goemba, and dress for real cold.
intro: From Paro town the Haa road leaves the valley floor at Bondey and climbs for about 30 km through blue pine, then spruce, fir and rhododendron, until the trees thin out at the top of the ridge. This is Chele La, at about 3,988 m, crowded with long poles of prayer flags snapping in the wind. It is generally called the highest pass on Bhutan's road network, and you feel it: the air is thin, the wind is cold even in May, and anyone who has come straight from the plains should walk slowly.

On a clear morning, the reason to come is to the north: Jomolhari, at about 7,326 m, the sacred mountain on the Bhutan–Tibet border, with Jichu Drake beside it. Below to the west lies the Haa valley, and to the east the Paro valley you have just left. The views are best from October to December and in spring before the cloud builds; by late morning, and for much of the monsoon, the pass can sit in fog and you see only flags and mist.

Most travellers cross Chele La on the way from Paro to Haa, or come up for a few hours as a half-day trip from Paro. There is nothing to buy at the top except, sometimes, a vendor or two in season, and no toilets worth the name, so plan around that. Haa needs a route permit and Chele La sits on the way, so the pass is reached with your guide and Bhutan-registered vehicle. Snow can close the road for hours or days in winter; check current status before you travel.

story.title: Flags in the wind
paras: The thousands of flags at Chele La are not decoration. They are lungta, 'wind horse' prayer flags, printed with prayers and mantras, and the Bhutanese belief is that the wind carries the prayers across the land as the flags flap, spreading blessings to all beings. The coloured strings, in blue, white, red, green and yellow, stand for the elements. The tall white flags on poles, called darchor, are often raised in groups of 108 in memory of someone who has died, to help their passage.

High passes are favoured places for flags because they catch the most wind and are where travellers have always stopped to give thanks for a safe climb. Bhutanese families drive up to Chele La to put up flags on auspicious days, sometimes with a monk to bless them first. You may see a family tying a new string between poles while the old ones, faded and torn, are left to wear away; burning or throwing old flags on the ground is avoided.

If you want to put up flags yourself, your guide can help you buy them in Paro and choose an appropriate spot, and will explain the right way to raise them. Do not take flags as souvenirs or walk on fallen ones. The pass is also an old crossing: before the road was built, people walked between the Paro and Haa valleys over this ridge, and the road follows a route that farmers and traders used for generations.
story.source: Prayer flag article (Wikipedia); Department of Tourism, Bhutan; common Bhutanese practice as explained by licensed guides

did_you_know: At about 3,988 m, Chele La is generally described as the highest motorable road pass in Bhutan.
On clear days the pass gives views of Jomolhari, at about 7,326 m one of Bhutan's most sacred mountains, on the border with Tibet.
Haa valley, on the far side of Chele La, was opened to foreign tourists only in 2002.
facts: Prayer flags, Jomolhari views, Kila Goemba, the road to Haa

highlights.title: Jomolhari at sunrise
highlights.text: Leave Paro by 6–6.30 am and you reach the pass while the air is still clear. On good days Jomolhari and Jichu Drake stand out to the north above the forest. October to December gives the best odds; in the monsoon, cloud usually wins.

highlights.title: The prayer flag ridge
highlights.text: Long strings of lungta and tall white darchor cover the saddle and run up the slopes on both sides. Walk among them slowly, keep to the left of chortens, and do not step on fallen flags. Mornings, with the sun behind the flags, are best for photographs.

highlights.title: Ridge walk above the pass
highlights.text: A path climbs the ridge from the pass for views over both the Paro and Haa valleys. Even 30–45 minutes up gives you a wider view. At about 4,000 m, go slowly, turn back if you feel dizzy, and do it on your last days in Bhutan, not your first.

highlights.title: Kila Goemba below the pass
highlights.text: A small nunnery set into the cliffs below the pass on the Paro side, reached by a walk downhill through forest from the road. It is one of the oldest nunneries in Bhutan and one of the quietest places on a Paro trip.

highlights.title: Spring rhododendrons
highlights.text: From about April to early June, rhododendrons flower in the forest on the climb up from Paro, in reds, pinks and whites depending on altitude. It is the best time for colour on the drive, though views from the top are hazier than in autumn.

how_to_reach.text: From Paro town, the Haa road turns off at Bondey and climbs about 30 km to the pass, 1–1.5 hours by car. From Thimphu allow about 2.5–3 hours. Haa town is about 26 km beyond, another hour downhill. A Bhutan-registered car with driver costs about ₹4,500–6,500 a day, indicative 2026. Snow can close the road in winter; check current status before you travel.

Chele La is on the road to Haa. Your operator arranges the route permit from the immigration office in Thimphu on a working day if you are going on to Haa, and a licensed guide is required for both Indian and international visitors. Check current status before you travel.

Paro airport is about 40 km away, so you can be at the pass within 2 hours of landing, though we advise against going this high on your first day. Overland, enter at Phuentsholing and reach Paro in about five hours via Chhuzom before heading up to the pass.

where_to_stay: There is nowhere to stay at Chele La itself. Most people sleep in Paro and come up as a half-day trip or on the way to Haa. In Paro, Hotel Olathang is a reliable government-built budget-to-mid option and COMO Uma Paro a premium one, with many certified 3-star hotels and farmhouse stays in between. On the Haa side, registered farmhouse homestays and small certified hotels in Haa town make a good base if you want to cross the pass and come back the next day, and they put you closer to the pass for an early start.
costs: Prayer flags to hang, from Paro shops
₹1,200 / US$100 per person per night, check current status before you travel
budget_tip: Do Chele La on your way to Haa rather than as a separate Paro day trip; you pay for one day of car and guide instead of two and still get the pass at its best in the morning.
tips: Leave Paro by 6.30 am for the clearest views; cloud usually builds by late morning.
Carry a down jacket, hat and gloves even in May or October; it can be close to freezing at the top.
Do not go this high on your first day in Bhutan, especially if you flew in from the plains.
Use the toilet in Paro before you leave; facilities at the pass are very limited.
Keep to the left of chortens and do not take or step on prayer flags.

experiences.title: Early morning views of Jomolhari
experiences.cost: Free; car and guide as part of your day rate
experiences.summary: An early drive from Paro to the 3,988 m pass for the morning view north to Jomolhari and Jichu Drake, with prayer flags in the foreground. Back in Paro by late morning, or carry on down to Haa.
body: Mountain views in Bhutan are a matter of timing. At Chele La, the clearest hour is usually soon after sunrise, before warm air from the valleys pushes cloud up the slopes. That means leaving Paro by about 6–6.30 am, with tea in a flask, and driving up through the forest while the light comes up. You reach the pass in 1–1.5 hours.

On a good day, Jomolhari, about 7,326 m and one of the most sacred mountains in Bhutan, rises to the north on the border with Tibet, with Jichu Drake close by. Below you the Haa valley opens to the west and the Paro valley to the east. The flags give a foreground, and by 8 am the sun is high enough to light the snow. On cloudy days, wait half an hour; gaps often open and close.

October to December gives the best chance of clear skies. April and May bring rhododendron colour on the way up but more haze at the top, and June to September is often cloud from the start. Dress for cold and wind: down jacket, hat and gloves. If you are carrying on to Haa, this is the best way to start the drive; if not, you are back in Paro for a late breakfast.

faqs.q: Can you see Jomolhari from Chele La
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days, usually in the early morning. Jomolhari, about 7,326 m, and Jichu Drake appear to the north. The best months are October to December, with spring a second choice. Leave Paro by 6.30 am, because cloud often builds by mid-morning, and in the monsoon months the peaks are usually hidden.

faqs.q: What time should I leave Paro for Chele La
faqs.a: Leave by about 6–6.30 am. The drive takes 1–1.5 hours, which puts you at the pass between 7 and 8 am, usually the clearest time. If you leave after breakfast, you reach the top around 10 am, when cloud has often covered the high peaks. Take tea and snacks to eat at the top.

faqs.q: How cold is it at Chele La
faqs.a: Colder than you expect. At about 3,988 m it is often around 0–8 °C in the morning from October to May, with a strong wind, and below freezing in winter. Bring a down or fleece jacket, hat and gloves even in spring. In December to February, snow can close the road entirely; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Hike down to Kila Goemba nunnery
experiences.image_query: Kila Goemba nunnery Chele La Bhutan
experiences.summary: A walk from the Chele La road down through forest to Kila Goemba, a small nunnery built into the cliffs on the Paro side of the pass. It is one of the oldest nunneries in Bhutan, home to nuns who live a life of retreat and study.
body: Kila Goemba sits below Chele La on the Paro side, a cluster of small white buildings tucked against a cliff face high above the valley. It is one of the oldest nunneries in Bhutan and home to a community of nuns who spend their lives in prayer, study and meditation. The setting is the reason most visitors come: buildings wedged into rock, prayer flags, and a long view over forest.

The usual route starts from the pass or from a point a little below it on the road, and follows a path downhill through forest to the nunnery in about 1–1.5 hours. Your driver then meets you at the road below, so you do not have to climb back up. The path is steady and sometimes muddy, with roots and stones, but not technical. Good shoes and a walking pole help on the descent.

Remember that this is a home and a place of retreat, not a tourist site. Keep voices low, ask your guide before photographing nuns or entering any building, and leave a small offering if you visit the shrine. Visiting rules can change, and some areas are closed to outsiders. Combine the hike with the morning view at the pass for a full half-day.

faqs.q: How hard is the Kila Goemba hike
faqs.a: It is a moderate walk, mostly downhill, of about 1–1.5 hours from the Chele La road to the nunnery, on a forest path with roots and loose stones. The altitude, near 3,500–4,000 m, makes it more tiring than it looks. Your driver meets you below, so there is little climbing. Wear good shoes and carry water.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Kila nunnery
faqs.a: Yes, with a licensed guide, though it is a working nunnery and a place of retreat. Some buildings may be closed to visitors, and you should ask before photographing the nuns. Keep voices low and dress modestly. Your guide checks on the day whether a visit to the shrine is possible. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I combine Kila Goemba with Chele La
faqs.a: Yes, this is the usual plan. Drive up early from Paro for the morning view at the pass, then walk down through forest to Kila Goemba, and meet your car on the road below. It makes a half-day of about 4–5 hours from Paro. Do it after you have spent a few days at Paro or Thimphu altitude.

experiences.title: Walk the ridge above Chele La
experiences.summary: A walk up the open ridge from the pass, among prayer flags and dwarf rhododendron, for wider views over the Paro and Haa valleys. You can turn back whenever you like; even an hour gives you a better view than the car park.
body: From the flags at the pass, paths lead up the ridge on either side. The most common walk heads up the open slope, above the tree line, through dwarf rhododendron and juniper, with the Haa valley on one side and the Paro valley on the other. You gain height quickly, and after 30–45 minutes of slow walking the view opens up well beyond what you see from the road.

This is a walk where you decide how far to go. Some groups climb for an hour and come back; fitter walkers spend two to three hours exploring the ridge with their guide. There is no fixed destination, and the path can be faint in places, so stay with your guide. The air is thin at about 4,000 m: walk slower than feels necessary, drink water, and turn back if you get a headache, feel dizzy or breathless.

Do this walk at the end of your trip, after a few nights at Paro or Thimphu altitude, not the day after you arrive. Mornings are clearer and less windy. Wear boots or trail shoes, layers, a hat and sunscreen; the sun is strong even when it is cold. In snow, skip it or stay close to the pass.

faqs.q: Is there a hike at Chele La
faqs.a: Yes. Paths climb the open ridge from the pass on both sides, among prayer flags and dwarf rhododendron. You can walk for 30 minutes or for two to three hours with your guide, turning back when you like. The views over the Paro and Haa valleys widen as you climb. Go in the morning and walk slowly at this height.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk at Chele La
faqs.a: It can be. The pass is at about 3,988 m and the ridge goes higher. Most people are fine for a short visit, but a ridge walk on your first day in Bhutan raises the risk. Spend a few nights in Paro or Thimphu first, walk slowly, drink water, and head down if you get a headache, nausea or dizziness.

faqs.q: Can children and seniors visit Chele La
faqs.a: Yes, for a short visit by car, if they are well and have spent a couple of nights in Paro first. Keep them warm, limit time at the top to an hour or so, and skip the ridge walk if anyone feels breathless. People with heart or lung conditions should ask their doctor before going to about 4,000 m.

experiences.title: Raise prayer flags at the pass
experiences.best_time: Any clear morning; auspicious days if your guide advises
experiences.cost: ₹300–1,500 for a set of flags, indicative 2026
experiences.summary: Buy a set of lungta prayer flags in Paro and, with your guide, tie them on the ridge at Chele La. It is something Bhutanese families do themselves, and a respectful way to take part rather than only take photographs.
body: Bhutanese families often drive up to high passes to raise prayer flags, especially on auspicious days or to mark a birth, a new venture or the memory of someone who has died. The coloured lungta strings carry printed prayers that, in Buddhist belief, the wind spreads over the land. The tall white darchor on poles are often put up in sets of 108 for the dead. Visitors are welcome to raise flags too, if they do it with care.

The day before, ask your guide to take you to a shop in Paro that sells flags. A string of lungta costs from a few hundred rupees; a full set can cost more. Some families ask a monk to bless the flags before raising them, and your guide can tell you whether that is practical. At the pass, your guide helps you choose a spot where your string can be tied safely between poles or trees without covering others.

Tie the flags so that they hang free in the wind. Do not cut down or move other people's flags, do not step on fallen flags, and never burn them in the open. Once up, they are left to fade and tear over time, which is part of the meaning. Families often take a short moment of quiet or a prayer after raising them.

faqs.q: Can tourists put up prayer flags in Bhutan
faqs.a: Yes, with your guide's help. Buy a set in Paro or Thimphu, choose a high, windy spot such as Chele La, and tie them where they do not cover other people's flags. Your guide can explain the meaning of the colours and whether to have them blessed first. Do it with respect, as a prayer rather than a photo prop.

faqs.q: What do the colours of prayer flags mean
faqs.a: The five colours, usually blue, white, red, green and yellow, stand for the elements: sky or space, air or water, fire, water or wind, and earth, depending on the tradition followed. Each flag carries printed prayers and mantras, and the belief is that the wind carries their blessings. Your guide can explain the local Bhutanese understanding.

faqs.q: How much do prayer flags cost in Bhutan
faqs.a: A string of lungta prayer flags costs from a few hundred rupees in Paro and Thimphu shops, and a larger set about ₹300–1,500, indicative 2026. Tall white darchor on poles cost more and are usually put up by families for special occasions. Buy from a shop your guide trusts, and ask about having them blessed.

faqs.q: Is Chele La the highest motorable pass in Bhutan
faqs.a: Chele La, at about 3,988 m, is generally described as the highest motorable pass in Bhutan. It sits on the road between Paro and Haa. Other well-known road passes, such as Dochula at about 3,100 m and Pele La at about 3,390 m, are lower. Exact heights given in different sources vary by a few metres.

faqs.q: How far is Chele La from Paro
faqs.a: About 35–40 km from Paro town, or 1–1.5 hours by car. The Haa road leaves the Paro valley at Bondey and climbs through forest to the pass. From Paro airport it is a similar distance. Haa town is about 26 km beyond the pass, another hour's drive downhill.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Chele La
faqs.a: Chele La is on the road to Haa, and Haa needs a route permit, which your operator gets from the immigration office in Thimphu on a working day. If you only go up to the pass and return to Paro, ask your operator about current rules. A licensed guide is required for both Indian and international visitors. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Chele La open in winter
faqs.a: Usually, but snow can close the road for hours or days between December and March. When it does, traffic to Haa goes the longer way via Chhuzom. Early mornings can be icy even when the road is open. If you are travelling in winter, keep a flexible day in your plan and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Chele La
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest skies and the best chance of seeing Jomolhari. April and May bring rhododendron colour in the forest below the pass but more haze. June to September is the monsoon, with cloud and fog most days. In every season, go in the early morning, before cloud builds.

faqs.q: Is Chele La worth it on a short Paro trip
faqs.a: It is worth it if you have a spare morning and the weather is clear, and it is the obvious choice if you are going to Haa. On a 3–4 night trip with only one Paro day, most people choose the Tiger's Nest hike first. On a longer stay, Chele La makes a good second day out from Paro.

faqs.q: Can I get altitude sickness at Chele La
faqs.a: It is possible, as the pass is at about 3,988 m. Most visitors feel only short breath on a short stop. Avoid going on your first day in Bhutan, walk slowly, drink water, and come down if you get a headache, nausea or dizziness. People with heart or lung conditions should check with a doctor first.

faqs.q: Are there toilets or food at Chele La
faqs.a: There are very few facilities. You may find a basic toilet and, in season, a vendor or two, but do not count on it. Use the toilet in Paro before you leave, and carry tea, water and snacks. On the Haa side, the first proper restaurants and toilets are in Haa town, about an hour below the pass.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Chele La
faqs.a: Dress for cold and wind: a down or fleece jacket, a windproof layer, a warm hat, gloves and closed shoes with grip, even in spring and autumn. Add sunglasses and sunscreen, because the sun is strong at about 4,000 m. In winter, snow and ice are possible, so wear boots and walk carefully near the flag poles.
